headline: Round 9's SAR671m drilling commitment is the yardstick for Saudi Arabia's tenth licensing round
deck: The ninth round awarded 172 sites, 76 of them at auction, and tied the winners to two years of spending. That, not the qualified list, is what the tenth round has to match.
excerpt: Saudi Arabia has qualified 24 companies and consortia to compete for exploration licences across three belts covering about 13,000 square kilometres. The measure of the round is not the list but what it commits bidders to drill, and the ninth round, which awarded 172 sites carrying more than SAR671 million of first-two-year exploration spending, is the yardstick.
content:
Saudi Arabia has qualified 24 local and international companies and consortia to compete for mineral exploration licences across three multi-mineral belts covering about 13,000 square kilometres, opening the competitive stage of the Kingdom's tenth licensing round, Arab News reported. The belts, the bidders and the choice of ground next to producing mines are covered in BrentDesk's report on the round. This piece is about how to judge it, because a qualified list is the least informative number a licensing round produces.

Qualification is not an award. It is a pre-screening of technical and financial capacity that establishes who may compete. Sites are allocated at a later stage, and in the Saudi system contested ground goes to a multi-round public auction. Auctioning contested sites rather than allocating them administratively puts a price on prospectivity, which gives the ministry a market signal about which belts the industry actually rates, and it means no ground has changed hands at this stage.

The yardstick is the ninth round, which the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources concluded in January. It awarded 172 sites to 24 companies and consortia across three belts in the Riyadh, Madinah and Qassim regions, 76 of them through public auction, and the winners committed to spend more than SAR671 million on exploration in the first two years of their licences.

That committed work programme, rather than the number of licences or the size of the acreage, is the figure worth tracking from round to round. It is contractual, it is time-bound and it is denominated in drilling. A licence taken without a spending obligation can be held for its option value; a licence carrying a two-year programme has to be worked or surrendered. Whether the tenth round matches or exceeds SAR671 million of committed spending will say more about its success than the 24 names that have cleared the screen.

The rounds are the mechanism by which the government is trying to put private capital onto ground the Saudi Geological Survey has mapped but nobody has drilled to a modern standard. The ministry values the Kingdom's unexploited mineral resources at about SAR9.4 trillion ($2.5 trillion), which is an estimate of geological potential rather than of proven metal, and the structure of the programme, spending obligations plus auctions for contested ground, is designed to stop licences being taken and then sat on.

The composition of the qualified list is the other thing to read. Alongside Ma'aden are Canada's Power Metallic Mines, Indonesia's state-controlled PT Aneka Tambang, Australia's Danakali, Wildsky Resources, and Saudi companies including Emerald Sources Mining, Sahara Mining and Thurb Al-Hayya for Trading. The presence of foreign juniors and mid-tier producers is the part the ministry is most likely to count as progress. Exploration is a business that large established producers are structurally poor at and specialist explorers are structurally good at, and a licensing regime that attracts only national champions tends to generate mine extensions rather than discoveries.

Spending is moving in the direction the programme needs. National exploration expenditure has risen to about SAR1.05 billion a year, roughly five times the level of four years earlier, but from a very low base, and much of the acreage on offer in this round has not been systematically explored. The measure of success is metres drilled and, eventually, discoveries, and neither is visible for years. The ministry has not said when block selection will close or when licences will be issued.
